st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The Practice Note accepts the cluster’s core proposition that generative AI should be deployed selectively within human-led, verifiable workflows rather than treated as generally competent or autonomous. It materially develops that proposition into a use-context-specific court framework: permitting bounded administrative and drafting assistance, restricting sensitive evidentiary and expert uses, requiring independent verification, preserving professional accountability, and providing disclosure, recordkeeping and periodic review.

kp.k: Court rules distinguish substantive generation from other legal technology
kp.d: Issued on 28 January 2025 and applying to all proceedings from 3 February 2025, the Practice Note covers both closed-source and open-source large language models used by practitioners and unrepresented parties. It excludes functionality that merely corrects spelling or grammar, transcribes, translates or formats without generating substantive content, as well as conventional search engines and the specified dedicated legal research search functionality. These are regulatory boundaries, not empirical findings about technology performance.
qs: This Practice Note applies to both closed-source and open-source large language model Gen AI.
This Practice Note is directed to the circumstances where such use is acceptable.

kp.k: AI risks include fabrication, bias, confidentiality and copyright
kp.d: The Court warns practitioners and unrepresented parties about plausible but inaccurate or fictitious output, fabricated references, incomplete or outdated datasets, jurisdictionally irrelevant material and bias. It also identifies risks that prompts become available to other users, confidential or privileged material lacks adequate protection, and training data was obtained in breach of copyright. These are stated potential risks, without measured error rates or evidence of their frequency.
qs: Examples include false citations and fabricated legislative, case or other secondary references;

Legal practitioners and unrepresented parties should also be aware that data entered into Gen AI programs may be used to train the large language model, potentially making confidential information available to others.

kp.k: Protected litigation information requires controlled, non-training AI environments
kp.d: Paragraph 9A prohibits entering information covered by suppression or non-publication orders, the implied Harman undertaking, subpoenas or statutory publication prohibitions unless the responsible practitioner or person is satisfied that the specified safeguards apply. These require a controlled environment with supplier confidentiality restrictions, no public availability or model training, and use only for the proceeding, subject to the stated legal-disclosure and law-enforcement exceptions.
qs: is not used to train the Gen AI program and/or any large language model.
is to be used only in connection with that proceeding (unless otherwise required or permitted by law to be disclosed or required to be reviewed by a law enforcement agency for policy purposes);

kp.k: Preparatory and analytical litigation tasks may use AI
kp.d: Subject to paragraph 9A, paragraph 9B expressly permits AI-generated chronologies, indexes and witness lists; preparation of briefs or draft Crown Case Statements; document and transcript summarisation or review; and written submissions or summaries of argument. The latter remain subject to additional verification requirements. The Note authorises these uses but does not quantify productivity gains or workforce effects.
qs: the generation of chronologies, indexes and witness lists;
the preparation of briefs or draft Crown Case Statements;
the summarising or review of documents and transcripts;

kp.k: Witness evidence must remain human-authored and unaltered
kp.d: Paragraphs 10–12 prohibit generating affidavit, witness statement and character reference content, other material reflecting witness evidence or opinion, and other material tendered in evidence or used in cross examination. AI must not alter or rephrase written witness evidence. Work merely preparatory to drafting the witness’s evidence or opinion is expressly permitted.
qs: Affidavits, witness statements, character references should contain and reflect a person’s own knowledge, not AI-generated content.
Gen AI must not be used for the purpose of altering, embellishing, strengthening or diluting or otherwise rephrasing a witness’s evidence when expressed in written form.
This paragraph does not prohibit the use of Gen AI for work that is merely preparatory to the drafting of the affidavit or other document setting out the witness’ evidence and/or opinion.

kp.k: Witness documents require non-use disclosures, with limited exhibit exceptions
kp.d: Affidavits, witness statements and character references must disclose that AI was not used to generate their content, including rephrasing evidence, or relevant annexures and exhibits prepared by the deponent for their evidence, subject to leave. Annexures or exhibits not created for the proceedings do not require the paragraph 13(b) disclosure. Exceptional applications to generate annexures or exhibits must identify the intended use, program and version, source and privacy or confidentiality settings, and benefit.
qs: In exceptional cases, leave may be sought to use Gen AI for the preparation or generation of any annexure or exhibit to an affidavit, witness statement or character reference.
the benefit to be derived from the proposed use of Gen AI in the preparation of the annexure or exhibit.

kp.k: AI-assisted submissions require verification beyond AI alone
kp.d: When AI helps prepare written submissions, summaries or skeletons of argument, the author must verify in the document that citations, authorities, case law and legislative references exist, are accurate and are relevant to the proceedings. Similar verification applies to references to evidence. AI alone cannot perform this verification, and AI use does not diminish professional or ethical obligations to the Court or administration of justice.
qs: Such verification must not be solely carried out by using a Gen AI tool or program.

Any use of Gen AI to prepare written submissions or summaries or skeletons of argument does not qualify or absolve the author(s) of any professional or ethical obligations to the Court or the administration of justice.

kp.k: AI-generated expert report content generally requires prior judicial leave
kp.d: Subject to paragraph 23, drafting or preparing any part of an expert report using AI requires prior leave. Applications must specify the proposed use, program and version, source and privacy or confidentiality settings, expected benefit, and documents to be submitted. The Court frames expert reports as the expert’s own opinions and reasoning; illustrative AI uses include analysis of sound, graphics or video, interrogation of very large datasets and statistical analysis.
qs: Expert reports are required to state the opinion or opinions of the expert, and his or her reasoning process.
Subject to paragraph 23 below, Gen AI must not be used to draft or prepare the content of an expert report (or any part of an expert report) without prior leave of the Court.

kp.k: Permitted expert AI use requires disclosure and records
kp.d: Experts granted leave must identify the report portions prepared using or drawing on AI material and name the program and version. They must retain records and annex an account of tool use, including prompts, defaults and variables, unless the Court dispenses with that requirement. Relevant binding or applicable AI codes or principles must be identified and annexed. Practitioners and unrepresented parties must alert experts to the Note when instructing them.
qs: disclose in the report what part(s) of it was prepared using Gen AI or drawing upon Gen AI produced material and the Gen AI program, (and version) that was used;
Legal practitioners and unrepresented parties must draw the requirements of this Practice Note to the attention of experts when instructing them.

kp.k: Specified expert reports have distinct timing requirements
kp.d: For professional negligence reports filed and served under UCPR rule 31.36 and the specified pre-filing work injury damages reports under section 315 of the Workplace Injury Management and Workers Compensation Act 1998 (NSW), leave to rely on AI-prepared or AI-informed reports must be sought at the first directions hearing. Reports prepared between the Note’s issue and commencement dates must identify any parts relying on AI.
qs: leave to rely on any report that was prepared using Gen AI or drawing upon Gen AI produced material must be sought at the first directions hearing of the matter.

Expert reports prepared between the date of issue of this Practice Note and the date of its commencement must identify which, if any, part or parts of the report has or have relied upon Gen AI in the preparation of its content.

kp.k: Court anticipates revising rules as AI develops
kp.d: Paragraph 26 commits to periodic review because AI is rapidly developing. The appended resources page, last updated 23 March 2026, records a review invitation for professional submissions by Thursday 18 December 2025. This establishes an ongoing review process, not evidence that the substantive requirements reproduced here were subsequently changed.
qs: Due to the rapidly developing nature of Gen AI, this Practice Note will be periodically reviewed.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Supreme Court of New South Wales recognises Gen AI as an aid to litigation preparation, while prescribing boundaries rather than predicting market or workforce changes.
pts.d: The Practice Note, issued by Chief Justice A S Bell, states that Gen AI can assist lawyers and unrepresented parties with drafting and summarisation. Paragraph 9B expressly permits chronologies, indexes, witness lists, briefs, draft Crown Case Statements, document and transcript review, and written arguments, subject to information safeguards and applicable verification requirements. It does not quantify productivity benefits or predict displacement, pricing changes or market restructuring.

pts.k: The Court identifies fabrication, unsuitable underlying data, bias and confidentiality risks as limitations of Gen AI in legal work.
pts.d: Paragraphs 7–8 warn that apparently authoritative output may contain fabricated references; underlying material may be incomplete, outdated, inaccurate or irrelevant to NSW or Australia; and outputs may be biased. Prompts and submitted information may enter training data or become available to other users. These are qualified risk statements, not measured error rates or findings about particular named products. The Note also flags potentially inadequate privilege and privacy safeguards and possible copyright breaches in training material.

pts.k: AI-assisted written argument requires verification that cannot be delegated solely to Gen AI, and authors retain their professional obligations.
pts.d: Paragraphs 16–18 require authors using Gen AI for submissions or summaries or skeletons of argument to verify in the document that authorities and references exist, are accurate and are relevant. Similar verification applies to references to evidence. This prescribes an assisted workflow with continuing author responsibility, rather than direct reliance on unchecked AI output.

pts.k: The Court limits AI substitution for witness evidence and subjects AI-assisted expert reporting to judicial permission and traceability.
pts.d: Paragraphs 10–15 prohibit Gen AI from generating witness-evidence content or rephrasing written witness evidence, while allowing merely preparatory work. Affidavits, witness statements and character references must disclose non-use, with specified rules for annexures and exhibits and exceptional leave for their generation. Paragraphs 19–23 generally require prior leave for AI-prepared expert-report content. Permitted use brings disclosure and recordkeeping requirements, including identification of the program and version and records of its use, unless the Court dispenses with the latter requirement. These are procedural restrictions, not empirical claims that all AI-assisted evidence is unreliable.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers judicial procedural authority and illustrative risks and uses, not empirical validation.
pts.d: The requirements derive from a Supreme Court Practice Note issued by Chief Justice Bell. Its capability and risk statements are not accompanied by studies, benchmarks, quantified outcomes, named sanctions cases or documented practitioner experience. Examples of false citations and expert uses illustrate the concerns and scope; they are not reported incidents or performance measurements. Statutory and procedural references specify the application of particular requirements. The appendix links further resources and speeches, but their substantive evidence is not supplied in this document.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The Note applies from 3 February 2025 and makes permitted use conditional on the technology, information and litigation task involved.
pts.d: Issued on 28 January 2025, the supplied Note applies to all proceedings from commencement and covers both closed-source and open-source Gen AI. It excludes merely non-substantive assistance such as spelling correction, transcription and formatting, as well as the specified search functionality. Paragraph 9A permits entry of protected or compelled material only if the responsible person is satisfied about a controlled confidential environment, proceeding-specific use subject to stated exceptions, and no model training. Expert reports in the categories specified in paragraph 23 instead require leave to rely on them at the first directions hearing. Reports prepared between issue and commencement must identify AI reliance. Periodic review is promised; the appendix records an invitation for review submissions by 18 December 2025 and a resource-page update on 23 March 2026, not a supplied replacement rule or prediction horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct subjects are practitioners, unrepresented litigants, submission authors, witnesses and experts in NSW Supreme Court proceedings.
pts.d: Practitioners and self-represented parties may use Gen AI for specified preparatory tasks but must manage input confidentiality and comply with evidence restrictions. Submission authors must verify AI-assisted references and retain ethical responsibility. Witnesses and deponents must provide their own evidence and the required non-use disclosures. Experts face leave, disclosure and recordkeeping requirements, and those instructing them must communicate the Note. The Court and administration of justice are expressly protected by continuing author obligations. No differentiated effects are claimed for firm sizes, ALSPs, in-house departments or legal-market segments, and permission for unrepresented parties is not presented as evidence of a reduced justice gap.
